### Two Council Members, One Unclaimed Problem

By Bay Tribune Civic

---

Mayor Avery Santana put the city's broad "citywide strain" onto the council agenda this cycle without attaching a sponsor — and watched two members reach for it from opposite sides of the chamber. Janae Rivers claimed it for the Oakland Progressive Party. Elliott Crane, the Civic Reform Coalition's District 6 member newly back in his seat, claimed it for District 6. An open problem rarely stays unclaimed for long. The question now is whether two hands on the same signal pull it forward or pull it apart.

### Query: "Oakland culture community neighborhood arts faith"

— CULTURE: **Faith Domain Running Hot Across Oakland** — Twenty-three faith-related events logged citywide this edition. St. Columba, Allen Temple, and Cathedral of Christ the Light all running at elevated community capacity. When the city is between policy and delivery, the churches fill the gap.

############################################################ LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
############################################################ Dear Editor, I manage the night shift at a parking garage on Broadway. Three times this month I've had to call 911 for someone in crisis on my floor — not threatening anyone, just lost. Shouting at nothing. Sitting in a stairwell shaking. The officers who show up are fine. They do what they can. But they're not trained for that and everyone involved knows it. The OARI pilot goes to West Oakland, Temescal, Fruitvale. I read the selection criteria — call volume, existing infrastructure, council cooperation. Fine. But Downtown has call volume too. My garage alone generates calls. The building next door generates calls.

---

Howard Young, a barista in Rockridge, put it simply. "I'm not a churchgoing person," he said. "But I know what the churches do. Everybody knows. When things get hard, that's where people go. Not city hall. The church." Brian Williams, a mechanic in Chinatown, echoed the sentiment from a different angle. "I go to temple sometimes," he said. "Not every week. But I know they're there. That's the thing — they're always there." They are always there. In a city that celebrates its diversity as a matter of identity, the faith communities are the infrastructure that proves it — not in statements or slogans, but in bags of groceries, blood pressure cuffs, tutoring sessions, and the steady sound of voices lifted together on a gray summer morning.
